title: Building an Autonomous Engineering Org - Angie Jones, Agentic AI Foundation

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's primary object is coding agents—Goose, Codex, and Claude Code—performing software-engineering tasks including code generation, bug fixing, PR review, and auto-fix loops at enterprise scale. Coding assistants like Goose and Codex are the central tools discussed, and the transformation of Block's 3,500-person engineering org grounds the content in enterprise operations. The described systems operate in production at enterprise scale, with agents actively shipping code through automated PR workflows and Slack-based delegation. The content covers enterprise-scale multi-agent orchestration, maturity models, and organizational transformation requiring advanced understanding of AI agent systems and engineering operations. This is a conference talk presenting a detailed real-world case study with quantitative results and specific system implementations. Multiple evidence anchors with quantitative metrics and concrete system descriptions directly support the coding-agents classification.

summary:
Angie Jones led the transformation of Block's 3,500-person engineering org into an autonomous one, also leading AI enablement for 12,000 employees across all functions. Block built Goose, their internal coding agent, before LLMs supported tool calling, and partnered with Anthropic as design partners for MCP. Despite 90% adoption of AI coding tools, the CEO noticed no shipping speed improvements, revealing a gap between experimentation and impact. Jones defines an agentic engineering org as one where engineers leverage AI agents as their primary means of producing engineering outcomes—treating agents as core team members who decompose problems, delegate work, and review results.

She created a 0-5 maturity model (inspired by Steve Yegge's Gastown article): Stage 0 (no AI), Stage 1 (autocomplete), Stage 2 (chatting, no PRs), Stage 3 (delegating tasks, reviewing output), Stage 4 (multiple agents in parallel), Stage 5 (full autonomous delegation producing shippable results). Most engineers were at stages 1-2. Jones applied the 1-9-90 digital community rule, forming an AI Champions program of 50 handpicked engineers from across Block's teams, each dedicating 30% of their time to AI enablement. Champions focused on making repos AI-friendly through context files, rules files, repeatable workflows, AI code reviewers, and AI attribution. After 3 months: AI-authored code up 69%, time savings up 37%, automated PRs up 21x.

Stage 4 introduced PR review bottlenecks as engineers tripled or quadrupled PR output. Solutions included enabling Codex on all repos with an auto-fix loop where a second agent automatically fixed identified issues before human review. Running multiple agents locally caused laptop memory and CPU exhaustion, leading to investment in dedicated cloud workspaces where each agent ran in isolation. A small group built Builder Bot, an orchestrator coordinating agents across a company world model of Block's 25,000-repo codebase—a machine-readable view of every service and its dependencies. This enabled agents to explore different system parts in parallel and assemble cross-codebase plans. Block reached stage 5, where anyone in the company could @build-a-bot in Slack to fix bugs or implement features without needing GitHub.

The talk ends on a somber note: layoffs followed, and Jones questions whether enabling employees to do incredible work ultimately resulted in their dismissal, leaving the audience with profound questions about the trajectory of autonomous engineering.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Context and the Adoption-Impact Gap
sections.summary: Jones describes Block's early agentic journey building Goose before tool calling existed, partnering with Anthropic on MCP. Despite 90% AI adoption, the CEO saw no shipping speed improvements, revealing the gap between experimentation and impact. Jones led AI enablement for 12,000 employees and was tasked with building an agentic engineering org, defined as one where engineers use AI agents as their primary means of producing engineering outcomes.

sections.title: Maturity Model and the 1-9-90 Strategy
sections.summary: Jones introduces a 0-5 maturity model (inspired by Steve Yegge's Gastown article) measuring engineer-AI delegation maturity. Most engineers were at stages 1-2. Facing challenges of no playbook, rapid tool evolution, and top-down AI fatigue, Jones applied the 1-9-90 rule, deciding to focus on the 1% power users rather than trying to level up all 3,500 engineers individually.

sections.title: AI Champions Program and AI-Ready Repos
sections.summary: Jones handpicked 50 engineers from across Block's teams (Square, Cash App, Afterpay, Tidal) to form an AI Champions program, each dedicating 30% of their time to AI enablement. They focused on making repos AI-friendly through context files, rules files, repeatable workflows, AI code reviewers, and AI attribution. Champions pressure-tested patterns across diverse repo shapes; monorepos used layered context, and mobile required different approaches from web. Teams chose what worked for their repo rather than receiving top-down mandates.

sections.title: Native Delegation Flows and Results
sections.summary: Champions enabled delegation from Slack, Jira/Linear, and GitHub issues. A Slack bug-diagnosis flow let Goose diagnose, propose solutions, and implement a fix in 5 minutes. Agents became part of sprints, and teams ran out of work. After 3 months: AI-authored code up 69%, time savings up 37%, automated PRs up 21x. The approach succeeded because delegation felt native to existing workflows.

sections.title: Stage 4: Multi-Agent Parallelism Challenges
sections.summary: Moving to stage 4 (multi-agent parallelism) was relatively straightforward given the delegation foundation, but it introduced PR review bottlenecks as engineers tripled or quadrupled PR output. Code reviews were already a struggle before AI; the problem worsened. Jones notes this is not fully solved but shares how they 'stopped the bleeding.'

sections.title: From PR Bottlenecks to Stage 5—and a Reckoning
sections.summary: To solve PR review bottlenecks, Jones enabled Codex on all repos with an auto-fix loop where a second agent automatically fixed identified issues before humans reviewed. Running multiple agents locally caused laptop memory and CPU exhaustion, leading to dedicated cloud workspaces where each agent ran in isolation. A small group built Builder Bot, an orchestrator coordinating agents across a company world model of Block's 25,000-repo codebase—a machine-readable view of every service and its dependencies. This enabled agents to explore different system parts in parallel and assemble cross-codebase plans. Block reached stage 5, where anyone could @build-a-bot in Slack to fix bugs or implement features without GitHub. The talk ends somberly—layoffs followed, and Jones questions whether enabling incredible work ultimately caused dismissals, leaving the audience with profound questions about the trajectory of autonomous engineering.

demonstrations: Slack-based bug diagnosis flow: engineer reported bug, another @goose in Slack, Goose pulled repo files, confirmed bug, proposed 3 solution options with code snippets, team aligned on option 1, Goose implemented it and returned PR link—entire cycle took ~5 minutes
Assigning Linear and Jira tickets and GitHub issues to agents for end-to-end implementation
Layered context approach for JVM monorepos: shared contexts/rules at root, specific ones at service levels
Champions program covering diverse repos across Square, Cash App, Afterpay, Tidal—frontend, backend, mobile, data, infra
Codex auto-fix loop: AI code reviewer identifies issues in a PR, another agent automatically fixes and commits them before human review
Builder Bot orchestrating multiple agents exploring different parts of the system in parallel, then assembling cross-codebase plans
Anyone at the company could @build-a-bot in Slack to fix a bug or implement a new feature without needing GitHub access
limitations: No playbook exists for building agentic engineering orgs—organizations are making it up as they go
Best practices become outdated quickly as new tools or models are released weekly, causing AI fatigue
Top-down AI mandates create resistance among engineers
PR review bottleneck at stage 4 addressed via AI reviewers and auto-fix but not fully solved
Most engineers remained at stages 1-2 despite high adoption rates
Early agent-generated code often didn't conform to team conventions and standards
AI's non-deterministic nature discourages many engineers who expect out-of-the-box reliability
Running multiple agents locally exhausts laptop memory and CPU
The transformation ultimately coincided with layoffs, raising ethical questions about the end goal of autonomous engineering
